title: Antibiotics and Resistance
hook: Antibiotics are among medicine's greatest tools — but every time we use one, the surviving bacteria get a chance to learn how to beat it.
key_points: Antibiotics kill bacteria or stop them from multiplying, but do nothing to viruses.
They work by attacking structures unique to bacterial cells.
Resistance arises when bacteria survive a drug and pass on their defenses.
Overuse and misuse of antibiotics speed up the rise of resistant bacteria.
content_html: Antibiotics changed medicine. Before them, a minor infection could turn deadly; today, drugs like penicillin clear bacterial illnesses that once killed routinely. They work by exploiting features unique to bacterial cells — bursting their walls or jamming their protein factories — which is exactly why they're useless against viruses, whose machinery is entirely different.
extra_html: The catch is that bacteria fight back. No drug kills every single cell, and the few that survive — those carrying chance mutations or borrowed genes that blunt the antibiotic — go on to multiply. Over many rounds of treatment, a population can become almost entirely resistant, leaving the drug powerless. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention explains that overusing antibiotics, including taking them for viral colds where they can't help, hands bacteria more opportunities to adapt. That's why using these drugs only when truly needed, and exactly as prescribed, is now a public-health priority worldwide.

source.name: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

related.title: What Are Bacteria?
related.hook: Single-celled and everywhere — in soil, oceans, and your gut — bacteria run much of the planet's chemistry, and most of them never make you sick.

related.title: The Human Microbiome
related.hook: You're never alone: trillions of bacteria, fungi, and other microbes live in and on your body, and most of them are working in your favor.

flashcards.prompt: Why don't antibiotics work against viruses?
flashcards.back_html: Antibiotics attack structures unique to bacteria — like their cell walls or protein-making machinery. Viruses are built differently, so the drugs have nothing to target.

choices.text: Bacteria that survive a drug pass their defenses to new generations
Humans get used to antibiotics and stop responding
Viruses teach bacteria how to resist

flashcards.explanation_html: When an antibiotic doesn't wipe out every bacterium, the survivors — those with resistance traits — multiply and spread, so the drug works less and less well over time.

flashcards.prompt: What speeds up the rise of antibiotic resistance?

choices.text: Finishing a prescribed course exactly as directed
Avoiding antibiotics when they aren't needed

flashcards.explanation_html: Taking antibiotics when they aren't needed, or not as directed, gives more bacteria the chance to survive and evolve resistance — which is why doctors urge careful use.
